source.title: Neural Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Michael Y. Hu; Jane Pan; Ayush Jhaveri; Nicholas Lourie; Kyunghyun Cho

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream-accuracy predictability using trajectory forecasting on held-out language-model runs, rather than testing the original pretraining-loss power-law or compute-allocation measurements.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates forecasts of downstream accuracy and reports their errors. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling against parameters, tokens or compute, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Background discussion and cited results about those topics are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well downstream accuracy can be forecast from early training trajectories or from average validation loss. It does this across DataDecide 90M–1B, Pythia 70M–12B and OLMo-Hybrid-7B runs, and reports errors against a trivial mean-accuracy predictor. It argues that per-task downstream scaling is predictable only with flexible, non-parametric forecasters, and that logistic loss-to-accuracy laws generalise poorly. That bears directly on V6 and restates it. It does not measure pretraining-loss power laws, extrapolation of loss, compute-optimal allocation, shape, other modalities, or exponent dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that flexible neural forecasting of downstream accuracy beats logistic, BNSL and LC-PFN baselines (1.99% vs 3.56% MAE) and generalises to unseen tasks, families, larger sizes and a non-transformer model. They attribute about 90% of the gain to replacing the parametric form with a neural predictor on accuracy trajectories, and about 10% to token-level losses. Average-loss inputs add nothing. They argue that limits of downstream scaling laws come from restricted hypothesis classes, not from the problem itself.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a neural trajectory forecaster trained on open-source checkpoints, combining early downstream accuracies, compute gaps and token-level validation probabilities. It does not fit the original pretraining-loss power laws or estimate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Forecasting errors differ across generalization settings; LOGISTIC and BNSL incur around 4 times higher error on Pythia and OLMo-Hybrid than on in-distribution different-seed evaluations. N EU N EU is evaluated with the first 20% of each held-out run observed.

fits_no_version.finding: Token-level validation probabilities carry downstream-predictive signal beyond average loss. Going from NoLoss to NeuNeu gives about 10% of the error reduction, and average-loss inputs add nothing over accuracy trajectories alone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Average pretraining loss is an insufficient statistic for downstream accuracy; distributional loss information adds predictive signal.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), as stated in the text
record.problems: Evaluation is limited to open-source training trajectories and downstream classification accuracy; the authors note generative tasks may have different scaling dynamics. The reported main evaluation conditions cover only the checkpoints and task suite used in this study. Several baselines' aggregate numerical errors are not stated in the text, and the task table gives values averaged over settings rather than separate per-setting errors.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the remaining table columns (LC-PFN, BNSL, NoLoss and AVERAGE) at each individual task; their specific task-level values are presented in Figure 3(b), but the retained rows prioritize N EU N EU and LOGISTIC task comparisons. The text also discusses that neural methods outperform baselines and that errors vary with extrapolation horizon, but does not provide corresponding exact values in the prose.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute; not measured.
Extrapolation of loss fits from small to large runs; loss is supplied as ground truth, not predicted.
Effects of depth, width or shape at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Generative tasks. Prediction of large-model downstream accuracy from small models alone: every forecast sees the first 20% of the target run. Logistic laws composed with a loss-from-compute law.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Mean-accuracy trivial predictor MAE per task, the baseline for all task rows (e.g. ARC-C 0.0529, BoolQ 0.0703, MMLU 0.0387)
Per-setting MAE (new seed, new data C4, Pythia, OLMo-Hybrid) for all methods; only plotted
Held-out-task result: NeuNeu MAE on 13 unseen tasks decreases slightly and stays below logistic laws fit to those tasks
Error versus extrapolation horizon on 1B runs: neural methods stay low, parametric baselines higher
Per-task LC-PFN, BNSL, NoLoss and Average values, including cases worse than the mean predictor

record.verdict_notes: Predictability here is within-run, over training compute: every forecast conditions on the first 20% of the target run. Logistic and BNSL receive ground-truth future average loss, so their errors understate a realistic pipeline. Subjects in all rows are forecasters; the language models forecast are DataDecide 90M–1B, Pythia 70M–12B and OLMo-Hybrid-7B. Not an original source. The record's reader-assigned T2 is changed to T5 because the paper argues V6 needs restating (no single parametric family fits per-task downstream scaling).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
Effects of depth, width and other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning or transfer.
Tests forecasts of downstream classification accuracy from early observed trajectories; does not test downstream generative tasks or establish a general relationship from pretraining loss alone.
Does not fit or compare pretraining-loss power-law exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups. Its downstream-accuracy forecasting results do not test those claims.

relationships.condition: Forecasting downstream classification accuracy from the first 20% of a run's accuracy trajectory plus token-level probabilities, on DataDecide, Pythia and OLMo-Hybrid runs
relationships.reason: Aggregate MAE is 1.99% (R1). Per-task MAE is roughly 2–13x below the mean-predictor baseline on most OLMES tasks (R7, R9, R13, R15, R17, R19, R21, R23, R25). Final-performance ranking accuracy is 0.766 (R27).
relationships.display_finding: Forecasts achieved 1.99% aggregate mean absolute error, roughly 2–13 times lower per-task error than the mean-predictor baseline on most OLMES tasks, and 0.766 final-performance ranking accuracy.
